newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries quiet in London, hold top of range.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries quiet in London, hold top of range.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were quiet in London on Monday, with little to knock them off newly captured highs, traders said.
The data agenda this week is light and analysts said the market could drift higher in its currently comfortable environment of low inflation.
"It's quarter end, there's people looking for duration. The view is one of the economy slowing down, inflation has been good, there's nothing to back it up," a trader at a U.S. bank in London said.
The benchmark long bond was quoted at 99-16 at 0945 GMT, for a yield of 6.663 percent, unchanged from both Tokyo and the close in New York on Friday.
September T-bond futures were down 3/31 at 112-14 in automated trade.
On Friday, the yield on the long bond dipped to 6.64 percent, its lowest level since February 21. T-bond futures were aiming for the year's high of 114-08 on February 18.
The trader at the U.S. bank said 114-08 was the next target for the future contract.
The main focal points for the market this week will be the Conference Board's June consumer confidence index on Tuesday and the University of Michigan's final June consumer index on Friday.
Also, the Treasury sells $15.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $11.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
Dick Howard, senior economist at Bank Julius Baer in London, agreed the market could stretch a little higher.

"There won't be much to drive it through the week so perhaps it can add a tick or two but probably not a point or two," he said. "The dollar seems to have done reasonably well out of the G7 summit so that may be a slightly helpful influence."
The dollar/yen was quoted at 115.29/15.39, off a session high of 115.67 in the wake of the summit in Denver which downplayed Japan's burgeoning trade surplus.
But Howard said Treasuries would eventually have to tackle the issue of tight labour markets. The June purchasing manager and payroll reports next week would likely put pressure on prices.
"It's definitely lull before the storm time," he said.
